chapter: Harlem scene and race in music
title: Harlem Renaissance and jazz
summary: Carter was focused on music and thinks Renaissance figures looked down on jazz.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But these are the pitfalls of all these things. I want to come now to an important aspect, I believe, of the cultural life in Harlem, and by inference, and ramification in all of America, and that is what has become known as the Harlem Renaissance, the beginning of the 1920's and going through the 30's as well. Of course, the Harlem Renaissance was primarily, I think, a literary process, but I'm wondering to what extent the Harlem Renaissance, which was a phenomenon of black writers and artists, as well as white audiences coming into Harlem -- to what extent this touched jazz and music generally in your own experience.
Now I know that since that time, you had have heard of the Harlem Renaissance. Did you -- or what sort of

things were going on at the time, in your own recollection, not your recollection today, but your recollection of what was happening at that time. Were you aware, so far as you remember now, of anything going on of a cultural sort, tremendous excitement, something called a Renaissance, or something that went in to the Renaissance at the time?
Well, as you said, it was primarily a literary movement, or something in which a lot of literary figures were involved. Painters, or -- you know, artists.

At that particular time, the only art form in which I was interested was the music, you know, and I wasn't too aware of what was going on with the so-called Renaissance, and I wasn't, I feel, involved in it, other than, maybe unknowingly, you know, in the music, but I don't know what part -- I don't at this moment know what part music may have played in the Harlem Renaissance, I'd like to have your thoughts on that.

Well, I think, that -- as it has been written up, in recent years by scholars -- I think that's one of the aspects that they stress; that jazz music which was an expression of the black people at that time, didn't seem to figure in Harlem Renaissance very much.
No. It was -- I think by the people, you know, that were involved in the Renaissance, I think jazz was looked down upon.
Do you have any recollection from that period that would suggest that?
You mean something to support that opinion?
An incident or events or something? I mean things that you recall from that time.
I mean there's plenty of evidence that we now have which would be a different thing.
